question: What are the three basic rules of navigation every operator should follow to prevent collisions?
choice_a: Always travel at maximum speed, follow the shoreline, and use only radio communication
choice_c: Always yield to sailboats and ignore power-driven vessels
choice_d: Practice good seamanship, keep a sharp lookout, and maintain a safe speed and distance
explanation: The three basic rules of navigation are to practice good seamanship, keep a sharp lookout, and maintain a safe speed and distance from other vessels and hazards.
source_note: WA Boating handbook, Encountering Other Vessels

question: What is a 'stand-on vessel'?
choice_a: The vessel that should maintain its course and speed
choice_b: The vessel required to change course immediately
choice_d: The larger of the two vessels involved
explanation: A stand-on vessel is the one that should maintain its course and speed, while the give-way vessel takes early and substantial action to avoid a collision.

question: When two power-driven vessels are meeting head-on, what should each do?
choice_a: The larger vessel always has the right-of-way
choice_b: Neither is the stand-on vessel; both should keep to the starboard (right)
choice_c: Both should stop completely and wait
explanation: In a head-on meeting between two power-driven vessels, neither is the stand-on vessel; both should turn to the starboard (right) to pass safely.
source_note: WA Boating handbook, Navigation Rules, Meeting Head-On

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel must give way?
choice_a: The vessel that arrived first at the intersection always has the right-of-way
choice_b: The faster vessel always must give way
choice_c: The vessel on the operator's port (left) side is the give-way vessel; the vessel on the starboard (right) side is the stand-on vessel
choice_d: Neither vessel is required to give way in a crossing situation
explanation: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, the vessel that has the other on its port side is the give-way vessel, while the vessel on the operator's starboard side is the stand-on vessel.
source_note: WA Boating handbook, Navigation Rules, Crossing Situations

question: In an overtaking situation, which vessel is the give-way vessel?
choice_c: Neither vessel needs to give way while overtaking
choice_d: The vessel that is overtaking another vessel
explanation: In an overtaking situation, the vessel doing the overtaking is always the give-way vessel, and the vessel being overtaken is the stand-on vessel, regardless of vessel type.
source_note: WA Boating handbook, Navigation Rules, Overtaking

question: In a power vs. sail encounter (with the sailboat not overtaking), which vessel is the give-way vessel?
choice_a: The powerboat is always the give-way vessel; the sailboat is the stand-on vessel
choice_b: The sailboat is always the give-way vessel
choice_c: Whichever vessel is moving faster must give way
choice_d: Neither vessel needs to give way
explanation: When a powerboat encounters a sailboat under sail, the powerboat is the give-way vessel and the sailboat is the stand-on vessel, unless the sailboat is overtaking the powerboat.

question: Describe a vessel's 'danger zone' used to identify who is the stand-on vessel in a crossing situation.
choice_a: Any area within 500 feet of your vessel in any direction
choice_b: The area from straight ahead of your vessel to 22.5 degrees beyond the middle of the vessel on the starboard side, the same area covered by your green sidelight
choice_c: Only the area directly behind your vessel
choice_d: The area covered by your red sidelight on the port side
explanation: The danger zone spans from straight ahead to 22.5 degrees aft of the beam on the starboard side -- the same area lit by the green sidelight -- and a vessel in that zone is the stand-on vessel.

question: When operating a power-driven vessel, which vessels must you give way to regardless of the normal crossing/meeting rules?
choice_a: Only vessels flying a distress flag
choice_b: Only vessels that are larger than yours
choice_c: A vessel not under command (such as anchored or disabled), a vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, a vessel engaged in commercial fishing, and a sailboat under sail (unless it is overtaking)
choice_d: You never have to give way if you are the faster vessel
explanation: Power-driven vessels must give way to vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, vessels engaged in commercial fishing, and sailboats under sail (unless the sailboat is overtaking).
source_note: WA Boating handbook, Encountering Vessels With Limited Maneuverability

question: If you must turn to avoid another vessel, how should you make the turn?
choice_a: As small and subtle as possible so as not to alarm anyone
choice_b: Only at the last possible moment
choice_c: Turns to avoid collision are discouraged; stopping is always preferred
choice_d: Large enough to be clearly noticed by the other vessel
explanation: If you turn to avoid a collision, make the turn large enough that the other vessel clearly notices it, since both operators share responsibility for avoiding a collision.
source_note: WA Boating handbook, Encountering Other Vessels

question: How should you behave when sharing the water with non-motorized vessels like canoes and kayaks, which sit low and are hard to see?
choice_a: Keep a careful watch, keep your distance, slow down when passing close, and give plenty of room and time since they move slower and are more affected by your wake
choice_b: Assume they will always move out of your way since they are slower
choice_c: Pass as close as possible to save time
choice_d: There is no special consideration needed for non-motorized vessels
explanation: Non-motorized vessels sit low in the water and are hard to see, and can be capsized by a passing wake, so operators should watch carefully, slow down, and give them plenty of room and time.
source_note: WA Boating handbook, Sharing the Water With Non-Motorized Vessels

question: Even though right-of-way rules exist, whose responsibility is it to take action to avoid a collision?
choice_a: Only the give-way vessel is ever responsible
choice_b: Both operators are equally responsible for taking the action needed to avoid a collision
choice_c: Only the stand-on vessel is ever responsible
choice_d: Neither vessel bears responsibility if a collision occurs
explanation: Even though one vessel is designated stand-on and the other give-way, both operators share responsibility for taking the action necessary to avoid a collision.
source_note: WA Boating handbook, On the Water
